title: Ternary Operator and Default Values
summary: Choose a value inline with condition ? a : b, and supply fallbacks with ||, ??, and ??=.
intro: Often you do not need a whole if/else block: you just need one of two values. The ternary operator picks a value inline, and `||` and `??` fill in a default when a value is missing.

steps.title: The ternary operator
steps.body:
`condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` checks the condition and gives back one of the two values. It is an *expression*, so it produces a value you can store, print, or drop into a template literal. An if statement cannot do that.

```javascript
const age = 20;
const status = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";
console.log(status); // adult
```

Assigning a ternary to a `const` is the main reason to use it: with if/else you would need a `let` declared first and then reassigned in each branch.

Because it is an expression, it fits inside `${...}`:

```javascript
const lives = 1;
console.log(`${lives} ${lives === 1 ? "life" : "lives"} left`);
```

The condition is tested for truthiness, just like in an if. The ternary also has very low precedence, so `"Price: " + isMember ? 8 : 10` joins the strings first and prints just `8`. Wrap it in parentheses when you mix it with `+`: `"Price: " + (isMember ? 8 : 10)`.

Keep ternaries to simple two-way choices between values. If a reader has to stop and decode it, use if/else.

example.title: Plurals and parity
example.prompt: Pick the right plural for two counts, then say whether a number is even.
example.explanation: Each ternary checks its condition and hands back one string. `cartItems === 1` is true, so `cartWord` is `"item"`. `bagItems === 1` is false, so `bagWord` is `"items"`. The last line puts the ternary straight into the template literal: `8 % 2 === 0` is true, so it inserts `even`.

practice.title: Pass mark and member price
practice.prompt:
Use ternaries to pick a result and a price.

1. Using `score`, make a `const result` that is `"pass"` when the score is at least 50 and `"fail"` otherwise.
2. Print `Result: ` followed by `result`.
3. Print `Price: ` followed by 8 when `isMember` is true and 10 otherwise, choosing the number with a ternary inside the template literal.

Expected output:

```text
Result: fail
Price: 8
```
hints: `isMember` is already a boolean, so it can be the whole condition by itself. You do not need `=== true`.

steps.title: Chained ternaries

example.title: Sign of a number
example.prompt: Label a number as negative, zero, or positive.
example.explanation: `n < 0` is checked first. It is true for -4, so the whole expression is `"negative"` and the remaining conditions are never checked. For 0 the second line would win, and any other number falls through to `"positive"`.

practice.title: Temperature label
practice.prompt:
Label a temperature with a chained ternary.

1. Make a `const label` from `celsius`: `"cold"` below 10, `"mild"` below 25, and `"hot"` otherwise.
2. Write one condition per line.
3. Print one line: the temperature followed directly by the letter `C`, then the word `is`, then the label, separated by single spaces.

Expected output:

```text
18C is mild
```
practice.starter:
const celsius = 18;

// TODO: build label with a chained ternary, then print it
hints: Check `celsius < 10` first, then `celsius < 25`, then give the final value with no condition.
In the template literal, write `C` right after `${celsius}` with no space.

steps.title: Defaults with || and ??
steps.body:
`||` does more than give `true` or `false`: it hands back one of its two values. `a || b` gives `a` if it is truthy, otherwise `b`. That is a quick default, but it also throws away valid falsy values such as `0` and `""`.

`a ?? b` (nullish coalescing) gives `b` only when `a` is `null` or `undefined`. Use `??` whenever `0` or `""` is a real answer:

```javascript
const stock = 0;
console.log(stock || 10); // 10, the 0 is lost
console.log(stock ?? 10); // 0
```

Both have an assignment form that fills in a default in place. `x ??= value` assigns only when `x` is null or undefined. `x ||= value` assigns when `x` is falsy. Declare `x` with `let`, since it may be reassigned.

```javascript
let limit;
limit ??= 100; // limit is now 100
```

One gotcha: `??` cannot sit next to `||` or `&&` without parentheses. Writing `a || b ?? c` is a SyntaxError, and the program will not run at all. Add parentheses to say what you mean: `(a || b) ?? c`.

example.title: Volume and nickname defaults
example.prompt: Compare || and ?? on a zero volume, default a missing nickname, and fill in two variables in place.
example.output:
volume || 50: 50
volume ?? 50: 0
Name: Anonymous
Retries: 3
Label: untitled
example.explanation: `0` is falsy, so `volume || 50` skips it and gives 50, losing the valid setting. `volume ?? 50` keeps 0 because 0 is not null or undefined. `nickname` is `null`, so `??` supplies `"Anonymous"`. `retries` starts as `undefined`, so `??=` assigns 3. `label` is the empty string, which is falsy, so `||=` replaces it.

practice.title: Page settings
practice.prompt:
Fill in default settings for a page.

1. Print `Page size: ` followed by `pageSize ?? 20`.
2. Print `Title: ` followed by `title || "Untitled"`.
3. Print `Author: ` followed by `author ?? "Unknown"`.
4. Give `theme` the default `"dark"` with `??=`, then print `Theme: ` and its value.
5. Give `city` the default `"Paris"` with `||=`, then print `City: ` and its value.

Expected output:

```text
Page size: 0
Title: Untitled
Author: Unknown
Theme: dark
City: Paris
```

tests.output:
Page size: 0
Title: Untitled
Author: Unknown
Theme: dark
City: Paris

hints: Put each default expression inside `${...}` in a template literal.
`pageSize` is 0, which is a real value, so `??` keeps it. `title` is `""`, which is falsy, so `||` replaces it.

recap:
- `condition ? a : b` is an expression: assign it to a `const` or put it in `${...}`.
- Chain `a ? x : b ? y : z` for three or more values, one condition per line.
- Use if/else when a branch does more than pick a value.
- `a || b` replaces any falsy `a`, including `0` and `""`.
- `a ?? b` replaces only `null` and `undefined`, so use it when `0` or `""` is valid.
- `x ??= v` and `x ||= v` assign a default in place.
- Mixing `??` with `||` or `&&` needs parentheses: `(a || b) ?? c`.
